title: What exactly is the Peter Principle?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Peter Principle, the idea that employees get promoted based on competence until they reach a level of incompetence. They cover Dr. Laurence J. Peter's 1969 book (based on a 1967 Esquire article), the FEMA response to Hurricane Katrina under Michael Brown as an example, how the principle plays out in hierarchies, contrasting ideas from C. Northcote Parkinson (work expands to fill time) and Lazear's theory of decline, applying the idea to innovation, ways to avoid it (demotion without stigma, pay raises without promotion, Peter's Perry self-sabotage), and a listener mail about sleep paralysis and waking nightmares from listener Drowsy Doug.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat casually about old TV shows and Tim Conway before introducing the Peter Principle topic.

segments.title: Origins of the Peter Principle
segments.summary: The Peter Principle is introduced as a 1969 book by Dr. Laurence J. Peter, based on a 1967 Esquire article, and described as a tongue-in-cheek observation that people get promoted until they become incompetent.

segments.title: FEMA and Hurricane Katrina example
segments.summary: Michael Brown, previously head of the Arabian Horse Association judges commission, was FEMA head during Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and is cited as an example of being promoted beyond his competence, though the hosts note he was also connected to the president.

segments.title: How the Peter Principle plays out in hierarchies
segments.summary: Using a web developer who becomes a manager as an example, the hosts explain how skill sets differ between roles, how incompetent managers make poor promotion decisions, and how mediocrity sets in because demotion is rare.

segments.title: Ways to fight the Peter Principle and Parkinson's law
segments.summary: The hosts discuss remedies such as demotion without stigma and pay raises without promotion, Parkinson's law (work expands to fill time), and Lazear's theory that employees fake a work ethic to earn promotions.

segments.title: Peter Principle applied to innovation and Google
segments.summary: Nitton Bore Bore One Car's essay applies the same principle to innovation: companies hit a home run, stagnate, and innovators leave to start new firms. Josh and Chuck debate whether Google has stagnated.

segments.title: Peter's Perry and self-sabotage
segments.summary: Turning down promotions, called Peter's Perry, is discussed, along with self-sabotage examples such as wearing too much cologne or parking in the president's space.

segments.title: Wrap-up and transition to listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts close the Peter Principle discussion and direct listeners to HowStuffWorks for more, then move to listener mail.

segments.title: Drowsy Doug's waking nightmares
segments.summary: Listener Drowsy Doug describes sleep paralysis episodes where his mind wakes before his body and he sees frightening images, such as a figure in a pig suit. The hosts say it is a recognized condition and reference Donnie Darko.
